paragraphs: January in this catalog is a Southern Hemisphere and equatorial window: Aconcagua and Ojos del Salado sit in their high season, New Zealand’s volcanoes and Southern Alps are in austral summer, and Kilimanjaro plus Kenya still show as in season.

Mexican volcanoes (Orizaba, Iztaccíhuatl, Popocatépetl) and a handful of USA winter-access peaks round out the list. Antarctica’s Vinson season is already open from the November start in the catalog — treat it as an expedition calendar, not a casual hike.
Use the groups below as planning filters, then open each peak for permits, staging, and the 3D map. Always confirm the current season on the official land-manager page.
February keeps the austral-summer Andes and New Zealand lists open: Aconcagua, Ojos del Salado, Patagonian granite, and Aoraki / Mt. Cook remain in the catalog’s in-season set.

East African walk-ups (Kilimanjaro, Kenya, Meru) and Mexico’s high volcanoes are still tagged for this month. Northern Rockies and Sierra entries here are the year-round or winter-tolerant exceptions, not a USA summer season.
If you are shopping a first big trip, compare Kilimanjaro vs Aconcagua on difficulty and permits before you pick a hemisphere.
March is a shoulder between austral summer and the Himalayan pre-monsoon. Ojos del Salado, New Zealand, and Kilimanjaro still appear; Aconcagua has usually dropped off this catalog’s window.
Mexico’s volcanoes stay in season, and a few USA peaks with long or year-round access show up. Cotopaxi remains on the equatorial list.
Treat March as a bridge month: good for volcanoes and Southern Alps, thin for North American high-country walk-ups that want July snow-free trails.
April is when the Nepal/China 8000 m list lights up in this catalog — Everest, Lhotse, Makalu, Cho Oyu — alongside Annapurna, Manaslu, and other Nepal objectives in their pre-monsoon window.
USA coverage jumps as desert and lower peaks enter spring. Kinabalu, Irish hills, and Cotopaxi also remain. Southern Hemisphere high Andes are mostly out except a couple of New Zealand volcanoes.
This is a permit-heavy month in the Himalaya: the peak pages carry the access notes, not live lottery dates.
May is the catalog’s first big Northern Hemisphere expansion: dozens of USA peaks, UK and Irish hills, and the Nepal 8000 m list still in its pre-monsoon window.

Bolivian Cordillera peaks (Illimani, Sajama, Huayna Potosí) appear on the austral dry-season side of the calendar — winter there, not summer. Half Dome’s cables window is marked as a shoulder approximation (late May–early October).
If you want snow-free Sierra or Colorado trails, May is early; if you want Everest-region logistics, it is prime.
June opens the USA high-country majority and the Karakoram 8000 m window (K2, Broad Peak, the Gasherbrums, Nanga Parbat) in this catalog.

Alps and Pyrenees start to fill in. Equatorial and Indonesian volcanoes (Kilimanjaro, Rinjani, Puncak Jaya) stay in season. Andean entries such as Huascarán are austral-winter climbing windows, not Southern Hemisphere summer.
This is the month the atlas looks most like a global menu: Rockies, Sierra, Alps, Karakoram, and a thinner Southern list.
July is the densest month in the catalog — US 14ers, Cascades, Alps (Matterhorn, Mont Blanc, Eiger), Canada, and the Karakoram remain in season.

Do not read this as global summer: Huascarán, Illimani, and Sajama are on their Andean dry-season / austral-winter side. Kilimanjaro and Puncak Jaya are equatorial exceptions, not a July heat wave at 6,000 m.
If you want a classic Northern Hemisphere walk-up or alpine ridge, July is the default window this dataset encodes.
August stays close to July’s Northern Hemisphere peak: USA, Swiss and Italian Alps, UK hills, and Karakoram expeditions still dominate the counts.
East African and New Guinea objectives remain. Andean dry-season peaks continue; they are not midsummer outings south of the equator.
Late-August plans should still check snow on north-facing alpine routes and monsoon remnants on Nepal peaks that have already left this month’s list.
September keeps most USA and Alps peaks in season while the Nepal 8000 m post-monsoon list returns (Everest through Annapurna).
It is still a Northern Hemisphere high-country month in this catalog, with Bolivian and East African peaks continuing on their own calendars.
Shoulder labels appear on cables-season and “early September” windows — those are approximate, not a guaranteed snow-free date.
October thins the USA list to peaks with longer seasons and keeps the Nepal post-monsoon 8000 m set. Kilimanjaro and Meru remain on the equatorial side.
Alps and Rockies high routes that were July–September only have largely dropped. Half Dome’s cables window is still an approximate shoulder through early October.
This is a Himalaya-and-volcano month more than a Colorado 14er month in the catalog.
November flips toward austral spring and polar season: New Zealand, Patagonia granite, Table Mountain, and Antarctica (Vinson, Sidley) enter the in-season set.
Nepal trekking peaks (Ama Dablam, Mera, Island Peak) and Mexican volcanoes also show. USA coverage is the short-season leftover, not a fall 14er rush.
If you want ice and expedition logistics, this is the start of the Antarctic and Southern Alps chapter — not Northern Hemisphere summer.
December is austral summer in the catalog: Aconcagua, Ojos del Salado, New Zealand, Patagonia, and Ecuadorian volcanoes sit alongside Mexican high volcanoes.
Antarctica remains in season from the November open. USA peaks here are winter or year-round listings. Margherita and other equatorial African entries appear on their own windows.
Pair this month with the January page if you are choosing an Andes vs Kilimanjaro vs NZ trip over the holidays.
